extracted.intended_audience: general literate public / readers of The Spectator (early-18th-century moral and social commentary)
extracted.subtask_description: Short moral and social essays (The Spectator) discussing proper conduct, civic/customary norms, and private behavior — covering patronage, parental duty, lotteries, inheritance, and court levées. The page gives prescriptive observations and examples rather than formal scoring rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of worthy admiration
rubrics_metrics.description: The wise Man applauds him whom he thinks most virtuous; the rest of the World, him who is most wealthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admiration should be based on virtue rather than mere possession or wealth. The author contrasts vulgar admiration (for wealth and power) with the wise man's preference for virtue; warns that ordinary people admire what they themselves wish to possess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate audience for dedications / patronage
rubrics_metrics.description: It is usually ridiculous to give Dedications or address Performances to Men no way addicted to Liberal Arts; Dedications to ignorant Men are as absurd... the Panegyrick generally implies no more than if the Author should say to the Patron; My very good Lord, You and I can never understand one another, therefore I humbly desire we may be intimate Friends for the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should not dedicate works to patrons who cannot appreciate them — such addresses are both vain and ludicrous. Patronage should be sought where genuine appreciation or shared values exist; mismatched patronage reveals folly on both sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution in bestowing praise
rubrics_metrics.description: He that commends another engages so much of his own Reputation as he gives to that Person commended; and he that has nothing laudable in himself is not of Ability to be such a Surety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praising others risks attaching one's reputation to them; only those with personal merit should act as endorsers. implication: be judicious in public commendation and avoid lending credibility to unworthy persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental tenderness as moral duty (anti-cruelty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Was there ever such an Image of Paternal Tenderness! ... I have exposed this Picture of an unnatural Father with the same Intention, that its Deformity may deter others from its Resemblance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parental cruelty is monstrously wrong; representing such cruelty serves as deterrent. The essay uses a savage letter from a father as an anti-pattern and recommends reproach and satire to discourage such behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental obligations outweigh filial pride
rubrics_metrics.description: I must confess, in all Controversies between Parents and their Children, I am naturally prejudiced in favour of the former. The Obligations on that Side can never be acquitted...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should regard parental duty and the obligations parents bear as weightier than children's claims; filial disobedience is a serious social failing. The writer defends parental authority as foundational to social order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filial obedience as basis of government
rubrics_metrics.description: The Obedience of Children to their Parents is the Basis of all Government, and set forth as the Measure of that Obedience which we owe to those whom Providence hath placed over us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filial duty is presented as a civic virtue: obedience within the family models obedience to lawful authority. Failure of filial duty is linked to social degeneration; examples from foreign customs illustrate severe punishments for impiety as social safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humane provision for marginalised women (compassion for 'wenches')
rubrics_metrics.description: In Countries where Popery prevails... there are large Endowments given for the Incurabili, such as are past all Remedy, and are allowed such Maintenance and Support as to keep them without further Care till they expire... this manner of treating poor Sinners has, methinks, great Humanity in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Society ought to provide humane maintenance and support for women trapped in prostitution or degraded situations; pity and reform (not mere moral scorn) are urged. The letters from women of the town are used as testimony of harsh conditions and to appeal for compassionate reform and attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid living on contingent expectations (financial prudence)
rubrics_metrics.description: It should be an indispensable Rule in Life, to contract our Desires to our present Condition... If we anticipate our good Fortune, we shall lose the Pleasure of it when it arrives, and may possibly never possess what we have so foolishly counted upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not spend or style your life according to possible future gains (lotteries, reversionary prospects, hoped offices). Live within present means; anticipate future wealth only when actually in hand to avoid ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of selection by caprice or superstition
rubrics_metrics.description: When a Man has a mind to venture his Money in a Lottery, every Figure of it appears equally alluring... In this Case therefore Caprice very often acts in the Place of Reason... some choose numbers for superstitious or trivial reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions about risk (lotteries, choices) should not rest on irrational motives (birth-year, dream, numerological whims). The piece ridicules superstition-driven choice as an example of human reason misapplied to trivial matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value virtue and disposition of heirs over advancement or wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Good Habits are what will certainly improve a Man's Fortune and Reputation; but on the other side, Affluence of Fortune will not as probably produce good Affections of the Mind... An Estate in Possession of such a Successor to a good Man, is worse than laid waste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging the worth of offspring or successors, prefer moral character, industry, probity, valour and justice over rumours of advancement or mere fortune. The essay contrasts a worthy daughter's conduct with an heir who disgraces his father's name as an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental style: moderation and affability in upbringing
rubrics_metrics.description: I know not to what to attribute the brutal Turn which this young Man has taken, except it may be to a certain Severity and Distance which his Father used towards him... the Cornelii ... live with his Sons like their eldest Brother, and the Sons converse with him as if they did it for no other Reason but that he is the wisest Man of their Acquaintance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive severity and coldness can alienate children; a moderate, affable, companionate parental style (living with children as friend/brother) fosters better outcomes. Good example and affectionate correspondence multiplies charity and virtue within a family.

rubrics_metrics.name: Levée etiquette and purpose (substance over ostentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: It would not methinks be amiss to give an Account of that Market for Preferment, a great Man's Levée... the Business of a Levée is to receive the Acknowledgments of a Multitude, that a Man is Wise, Bounteous, Valiant and Powerful... this Commerce between the Mighty and their Slaves ... might do so much good as to incline the Great to regard Business rather than Ostentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court levées should be about conducting business, offering opportunities, and distributing patronage — not mere display. Patrons should be obliging, well-informed and give persons chances to exert themselves; clients should avoid servile ostentation and pointless attendance. Notes on dress/appearance (half-dressed military, reserved civil) and the staged etiquette are given as descriptive guidance and subtle criticism.
